questions.question: Triangle DEF is a right triangle with its right angle at vertex E. It is drawn upside down, so the right angle points down and to the right. DE = 9 cm, EF = 12 cm, DF = 15 cm. Which side is the hypotenuse?
options: DF, 15 cm, because it is opposite the right angle.
None of them, since an upside-down triangle has none.
EF, 12 cm, because it is the longest side lying flat.
DE, 9 cm, because it is the side pointing straight up.
questions.explain: The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle, whichever way the triangle is turned, so here it is DF, 15 cm. Turning a triangle upside down never changes which side is the hypotenuse.

questions.question: Triangle PQR has its right angle at R, and it is tilted so that no side is horizontal. PR = 5 m, RQ = 12 m, PQ = 13 m. Which two sides are the legs?
options: RQ and PQ, the two longest sides of the triangle.
PR and RQ, the two sides that form the right angle.
PR and PQ, the two sides that look most slanted.
It cannot be decided while the triangle is tilted.
questions.explain: The legs are the two sides that meet at the right angle, so PR and RQ; PQ sits opposite the right angle, so it is the hypotenuse. Tilting the triangle changes nothing about which sides are the legs.

questions.question: A triangle has sides 9 cm, 40 cm and 41 cm. Is it a right triangle?
options: No, because 9 + 40 = 49, which is not 41.
No, because 9² + 41² does not equal 40².
Yes, because 81 + 1600 = 1681, which is 41².
Yes, but only when the 41 cm side is drawn flat.
questions.explain: Square the two shorter sides and compare with the square of the longest: 81 + 1600 = 1681 and 41² = 1681, so it is right-angled. The common trap is adding 9 + 40 instead of adding the squares.

questions.question: A square is drawn on the outside of each side of a triangle. The square on the shortest side has area 36 cm², the square on the next side has area 64 cm², and the square on the longest side has area 100 cm². What can you say about the triangle?
options: It is not right-angled, since 6 + 8 = 14 and 14 is not 10.
It is right-angled only if the 100 cm² square sits at the bottom.
It is right-angled, with the 64 cm² square on the hypotenuse.
It is right-angled, with the 100 cm² square on the hypotenuse.
questions.explain: The squares on the two legs must add to the square on the hypotenuse: 36 + 64 = 100, so the triangle is right-angled and the 100 cm² square sits on the hypotenuse. The largest square is always the one on the hypotenuse, wherever it is drawn.

questions.question: Noor leans a ladder against a shed wall. The foot of the ladder is 2.4 m from the wall, the top touches the wall 7 m up, and the ladder itself is 7.4 m long. Is the triangle made by the ladder, the wall and the ground right-angled?
options: Yes, because 5.76 + 49 = 54.76, which is 7.4².
No, because 2.4² + 7.4² does not come to 7².
Yes, but only while the wall is standing upright.
No, because 2.4 + 7 = 9.4 m, which is not 7.4 m.
questions.explain: Square the two sides that meet at the right angle, the ground and the wall: 5.76 + 49 = 54.76, and 7.4² = 54.76, so the corner is right-angled. Adding 2.4 + 7 instead of squaring is the usual slip.

questions.question: Triangle KLM has its right angle at vertex L. Which equation must be true, no matter how the triangle is turned?
options: KL + LM = KM
KL² + LM² = KM²
KL² + KM² = LM²
KM² + LM² = KL²
questions.explain: The right angle is at L, so KL and LM are the legs and KM, opposite the right angle, is the hypotenuse: KL² + LM² = KM². Putting the hypotenuse on the left of the equation is the most common mistake.

questions.question: A garden bed is supposed to have square corners. Maya measures two sides meeting at one corner as 12 m and 16 m, then measures the straight distance between their far ends as 20 m. Is that corner a right angle?
options: No, because 12 + 16 = 28 m, which is not 20 m.
No, because 12² + 20² does not equal 16².
Yes, because 144 + 256 = 400, which is 20².
Yes, but only if the diagonal runs to the left.
questions.explain: The two edges are the legs and the 20 m distance is the hypotenuse: 144 + 256 = 400 = 20², so the corner is square. If you add 12 + 16 instead of squaring, you get 28 and the test tells you nothing.

questions.question: Two triangular flags are cut for a school field day. Flag A has sides 20 cm, 21 cm and 29 cm. Flag B has sides 20 cm, 21 cm and 30 cm. Which statement is true?
options: Both, as long as each is hung with its long side down.
Only Flag B, since its longest side, 30 cm, is bigger.
Neither one, since 20 + 21 equals neither 29 nor 30.
Only Flag A is right-angled, since 400 + 441 = 841.
questions.explain: Test each with squares: 400 + 441 = 841 = 29², so Flag A is right-angled, while 841 is not 30², so Flag B is not. Having a longest side does not make a triangle right-angled; only the matching square sum does.

questions.question: Ravi is building a small skateboard ramp. The back post stands 1.2 m tall, the base runs 0.5 m along the ground, and he has one piece of plywood 1.3 m long for the slope. Will the three pieces meet exactly, and which piece is the hypotenuse?
options: Yes; the 1.3 m slope is the hypotenuse, as 0.25 + 1.44 = 1.69.
Yes; the 1.2 m post is the hypotenuse, since it is the tallest piece.
No; 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.7 m, so the plywood sheet is too short.
No; tipping the ramp onto its back would change the answer.
questions.explain: The right angle is between the post and the ground, so the sloped plywood is the hypotenuse: 0.25 + 1.44 = 1.69 = 1.3², and the pieces meet exactly. The trap is calling the tallest piece the hypotenuse instead of the one opposite the right angle.

questions.question: At a campsite a tent pole stands straight up, 2.4 m tall. One rope runs from the top of the pole to a peg 1.8 m from the base and measures 3.0 m. A second rope runs from the top to a peg 3.2 m away and measures 4.2 m. Which rope, if either, is pulled perfectly straight, forming a right triangle with the pole and the ground?
options: Neither rope, since 1.8 + 2.4 = 4.2 m and not 3.0 m.
Only the 3.0 m rope, since 3.24 + 5.76 = 9, which is 3.0².
Both ropes, since a slanted rope still makes a right triangle.
The 4.2 m rope, since the longer rope must be the hypotenuse.
questions.explain: For each rope, square the peg distance and the pole height: 3.24 + 5.76 = 9 = 3.0² works, but 10.24 + 5.76 = 16 while 4.2² = 17.64, so that rope sags. Being the longest side does not by itself make a rope the hypotenuse of a right triangle.

questions.question: Tomas checks a triangle whose right angle is at the top-left corner. The two sides meeting there measure 7 cm and 24 cm, and the third side measures 25 cm. He writes 7² + 25² = 24² and says the triangle fails the test. What is the best response?
options: He is correct, because a right angle at the top does not count.
He should add the sides: 7 + 24 = 31, so it is not right-angled.
He used 25 cm as a leg; since 49 + 576 = 625, it is right-angled.
He mislabelled the 24 cm side, so the triangle is not right-angled.
questions.explain: The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, so 7 and 24 are the legs: 49 + 576 = 625 = 25², and the triangle is right-angled. Tomas squared the hypotenuse as if it were a leg, and a right angle in the top-left corner is still a right angle.

questions.question: Emma is marking out a corner of a rectangular ice rink. She measures 6 m along one edge and 8 m along the other edge from the corner, then measures the straight distance between those two marks as 10.5 m. What should she conclude?
options: The corner is square, since 6 + 8 = 14 m is more than 10.5 m.
The corner is not square, since 6² + 10.5² does not equal 8².
The corner is square; turning the rink would fix the extra 0.5 m.
The corner is not square; that distance should be 10 m.
questions.explain: The two edges are the legs, so a square corner needs a distance of √(36 + 64) = 10 m between the marks, and 10.5 m shows the corner is open too wide. Adding 6 + 8 tests nothing here, and turning the rink cannot change a corner from square to not square.
